title: Our Mutual Friend: A Literary Discussion

segments.title: Opening: The Dust Heaps and the City's Secrets

utterances.text: Welcome to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked — a close, unhurried journey through one of the greatest and strangest novels in the English language.
Our Mutual Friend was Charles Dickens's last completed novel, published in 1864 and 1865.
It is a book about money — where it comes from, what it does to people, and what people will do to get it.
It opens with a body pulled from the Thames and ends with one of the most satisfying reversals in all of Victorian fiction.
In between, Dickens gives us dust heaps, a golden dustman, forged wills, social climbers, scheming beggars, and a Society so hollow it rattles.
Joining me today are three people I could not be more delighted to have in the same room.
Dr. Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and creative writing teacher whose eye for how great prose is actually built — sentence by sentence, image by image — is unlike anyone else I know.

Oliver Trevelyan has narrated more classic novels on audio than perhaps any living person, and he hears Dickens's prose the way a conductor hears a score — the rhythm, the timing, the sheer performance of it.

And Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who first read Our Mutual Friend as a teenager and has returned to it more times than she can count — she brings the reader's love alongside the critic's precision.
We begin today where the novel's dark comedy begins — with the dust heaps, the money they represent, and the extraordinary parade of people that money attracts.
What strikes me first about these passages is the sheer structural audacity of routing the novel's social satire through the Secretary's letterbox.
Dickens doesn't show us the beggars directly — he shows us the paperwork they generate, which is a far more devastating choice.
It creates distance, and distance becomes comic, and comedy becomes indictment — all in the same move.
And then there's that list — fifty-seven churches, forty-two parsonage houses, twenty-seven organs — each denomination more absurd than the last.
Dickens is constructing a kind of satirical arithmetic — adding up the moral bankruptcy of Victorian charity in precise, ludicrous figures.
And then — the coup de grâce — that letter from the Duke of Linseed.
"Large fat private double letter, sealed with ducal coronet."
That word 'fat' is doing everything — it is physically repellent, morally bloated, and wickedly funny all at once.
Having read that passage aloud more than once, I can tell you that list of denominations is practically musical — it has a comic accelerando built right in.
But what I love — what I genuinely love — is the postscript on the Duke's letter.
Dickens calls it 'thoughtful in the postscript' — and the sarcasm is so straight-faced it takes a half-second to land.
That half-second is everything in performance — you let the audience find the joke themselves, and the laugh is twice as good.
Then the individual beggars in the next passage — Dickens categorises them with the thoroughness of a naturalist classifying beetles.
The 'daughters of general officers, long accustomed to every luxury of life, except spelling' — that parenthesis is a tiny perfect dagger.
And then the metaphor for their scraps of paperwork — he sets it up this way:
"they call their scraps documents; but they are, as to papers deserving the name, what minced veal is to a calf."
Minced veal to a calf — it's revolting, it's exact, and it's somehow completely right.
What keeps stopping me in these passages is the grief underneath the comedy.
The 'inspired beggars' sitting over a fragment of candle that must soon go out — that image is genuinely desperate.
Dickens is funny about them, yes — but the candle guttering in the dark is real poverty, and he doesn't let you forget it.
And the suicidal beggars with their precise deadline — 'a quarter to one P.M. on Tuesday' — is farcical, but only just.
That precision is the tell — it's the logic of someone who has run out of options and is trying to sound as if they haven't.
What I find fascinating is how this connects to the will passage — to what old Harmon actually left behind.
Wegg reads it out, and it's devastating in its brevity — here is the passage:

"Inasmuch as he has never made friends, and has ever had a rebellious family, he, John Harmon, gives to Nicodemus Boffin the Little Mound, which is quite enough for him, and gives the whole rest and residue of his property to the Crown."
'Never made friends.' 'Ever had a rebellious family.' The whole biography of a loveless man in two clauses.
Caroline is right that the will is where the comedy hardens into something colder.
'Quite enough for him' — four words that contain the entire contempt of a miser father for the one person he half-trusted.
But architecturally, what's brilliant is how Dickens uses Wegg as the vessel for this revelation.
Wegg is buoyant, self-congratulatory — 'I see I take you with me! Hear, hear!' — and the will he reads is a document of absolute human isolation.
The ironic gap between the reader and what is being read — that's Dickens at full stretch.
Wegg performing buoyancy while unknowingly narrating tragedy — that is a gift of a scene to read aloud.
There is a whole tradition of theatrical irony in which the speaker doesn't know what the audience knows, and Dickens plays it with total confidence here.
And the dust heap as legacy — the 'Little Mound' — is such a charged image.
A fortune built from refuse, inherited through death, fought over by schemers — the whole novel is compressed into that mound.
The dust heap as the novel's central symbol — fortune, filth, and everything society would rather not acknowledge piled up together.
We'll be returning to what that fortune does to those who inherit it, and those who scheme to take it.
But first, we'll turn to the river — the other great force running through this novel — and the lives it shapes and ends.

segments.title: Bella's Fall and Rise: The Mirror of Greed

utterances.text: Welcome to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked, the show where we take Dickens's last completed novel apart — with love — and examine every gear and spring.
Today's segment is called Bella's Fall and Rise: The Mirror of Greed.
We're looking at how Dickens constructs the moral architecture of this novel through characters who are defined — or destroyed — by their relationship to money.
Joining me today are three guests who bring very different lenses to this world.
Dr. Eleanor Hartley teaches creative writing and is a novelist herself — she is the person you want beside you when a passage's structural genius suddenly becomes visible.
Oliver Trevelyan has narrated more classic novels on audio than perhaps anyone alive, and he hears Dickens the way a conductor hears a score — every rhythm, every rest.
And Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who first read this novel as a teenager and has never quite put it down.
She is our conscience in the room — she will tell us when a character deserves better.

Eleanor, let's begin with you — because I want to start with the comic side of Dickens's obsession with identity and predestination, and Eugene Wrayburn has something astonishing to say on the subject.
Eugene's account of his father — M. R. F., the Most Respected Father — is one of those passages where Dickens's comedy is doing something structurally profound.
The joke is about a father who assigns his children's identities before the children have had the impertinence to be born and develop personalities of their own.
And the punchline is always the same — the child arrives, is forced into the designated role, and fails at it in precisely the way the role demanded.
Listen to the rhythm of this — Dickens builds it like a joke with three setups before the real sting:
That single word — shaky — does everything.
It's an entire career collapse compressed into one adjective.
And what Dickens is really setting up here is the broader theme of the novel: the tyranny of inherited roles — social, financial, moral.
What I love — from a performance point of view — is that Eugene is telling this story against himself.
He is one of the failed products of M. R. F.'s system — disposed of as a barrister and as a married man — and he narrates it with perfect, airy detachment.
That detachment is the character.
It's also, I think, part of what makes him both charming and slightly frightening as the novel develops — he has been so thoroughly un-invested in his own life that nothing touches him.
Until, of course, it does.

The line I always want to linger on is that third brother — appeared, considerably in advance of his engagement to my mother — which is the most exquisitely well-bred way of noting an illegitimate birth I have ever encountered.
Dickens trusts the reader completely there.
What strikes me, reading this alongside Jenny Wren — and I know we'll come to Jenny — is how differently Dickens distributes the cost of that same social machinery.
Eugene's dispossession from a genuine identity is a comedy, because he has the class and the wit to make it so.
For those without those protections, the same forces are simply tragedy.
But I do think Eleanor is right that Dickens is mapping something — the novel is full of people who have had their futures decided for them before they could consent.
Bella is the most obvious case — the girl left as a legacy in a dead man's will.
And that brings us neatly to Bella herself — and to a passage that is, I think, one of the most emotionally powerful in the novel.
Eleanor, R. Wilfer's blessing of Bella's engagement — what is Dickens doing there?
It's a rhetorical tour de force, and it works because Dickens has earned it.
Bella has been mercenary — genuinely, corrosively mercenary — for most of the novel.
So when her father calls her
— the word mercenary has been turned completely inside out.
It's now a term of the deepest honour, because she has chosen to be poor for the right reasons.
That is an architectural choice — the whole arc of Bella's development is compressed into the repetition of a single word used in two opposite senses.
When I've read that passage aloud — and I have, many times — the challenge is sustaining the cherub's glow without tipping into sentimentality.
What saves it is the legal precision of the language —
It sounds like a conveyancing document — and that's the joke, and also the point.
In a novel soaked in wills and inheritances and financial instruments, love is being formally ratified in the same vocabulary.
Dickens is saying: this is the real settlement.
I want to defend Bella for a moment — because I think she sometimes gets a slightly rough ride from readers who find her transformation too neat.
But her greed, early in the novel, is completely understandable — she was handed to a wealthy stranger as a bequest, like furniture.
Of course she becomes preoccupied with money — she has been told since childhood that money is the only thing that decides your fate.
What moves me in R. Wilfer's speech is that he is the only person in her world — perhaps the only person in the novel — who has always loved her without conditions.
And his blessing is the novel saying: here is what unconditional love looks like when it speaks.
And set against all of that warmth, we have what may be the novel's most chilling portrait of greed — Silas Wegg and his elaborate scheme against Boffin.
Eleanor, what is Dickens constructing in that extraordinary passage where Wegg lays out his plan?
The Wegg passages are a masterclass in how Dickens uses style to expose character.
The relentless repetition of
— that Pecksniffian self-congratulatory address — is doing comic work and sinister work simultaneously.
And then you get the word that crystallises everything — and Dickens makes it a one-word sentence, essentially:
That exclamation mark is doing so much work — it's greed performing its own entitlement, announcing itself as justice.
And then the plan escalates into something that reads almost like a parody of a legal brief — right through to the phrase about moral bondage.
Wegg is one of the great Dickensian grotesques, and he is a genuine pleasure to perform — but the darkness underneath is real.
Eleanor mentioned moral bondage — and that phrase lands differently once you realize it's the language of slavery being applied to financial extortion.
Dickens writes:
In a novel about inheritance and the corruption that follows great wealth, that phrase isn't just comic hyperbole — it's a structural diagnosis.
Wegg believes money gives him the right to own another human being's will.
What's so uncomfortable is that Wegg's logic isn't entirely unlike the logic of the wills and the inheritance system the novel spends so much time examining.
The difference between a legal will and Wegg's extortion scheme is one of legitimacy — and Dickens keeps making you question how legitimate the legal version really is.
The minion and the worm — those phrases Wegg uses for Boffin — are grotesque, but they're also what money does to the people it touches when the wrong people are holding it.
I want to bring us to two of the most remarkable passages in the novel — both concerned with suffering and guilt — beginning with Jenny Wren's vision.
Eleanor, Jenny's account of the children in white is extraordinary — almost visionary.
This passage is the emotional and spiritual heart of the novel for me.
Jenny Wren — a disabled child who makes dolls' dresses and who has, as her only parent, a dissolute drunk she calls her bad boy — is not who you'd expect to carry the novel's highest register.
But Dickens gives her this:
That double call —
— the repetition works like a psalm, like a liturgical refrain.
Dickens is writing a secular scripture for the most marginalized person in the novel — and he earns every word of it.
I can never read that passage without stopping.
What undoes me is the detail — the children who were not chilled, anxious, ragged, or beaten.
Because those four words describe what Jenny's actual daily life is.
The vision defines itself entirely by negation — by everything it withholds from her when she wakes.
And the promise of return —
— is both consolation and postponement.
The children are coming back — but Jenny is still in pain now.
Performing that passage is — I'll be honest — one of the harder things I've done, because you have to resist the temptation to make it beautiful.
The tone is something more stripped than beauty — it's the matter-of-factness of great suffering described by someone who has made a kind of peace with it.
That phrase — in a tone as though it were ages ago — is Dickens directing the performance right there in the text.
Jenny is a child speaking about her own childhood as if from a great distance.
That distance is the wound.
And now to the novel's darkest register — Bradley Headstone, and what happens to a man who commits violence but cannot feel remorse.
Eleanor, Dickens's analysis of Bradley's psychological state is almost clinical in its precision — and terrifying for it.
It's one of the most psychologically advanced pieces of writing in all of Victorian fiction, I think.
The standard moral machinery of the novel — guilt, remorse, confession, punishment — Dickens refuses it here.
Bradley has no remorse.
And so Dickens invents a worse punishment — one that is intrinsic to the crime itself:
He is condemned to rehearse the crime forever, and always to find new ways he could have done it better.
That is not redemption — it's a specifically modern vision of hell: obsession without release.
And then Charley Hexam walks in and delivers what might be the most withering speech in the novel.
Not to eulogise Eugene, not to avenge Lizzie — but to complain that Bradley has been inconvenient to Charley.
It's grotesque and it's also perfect, because it tells us everything about what class anxiety does to a person.
The accusation Charley lands on is:
He accuses a man who has just attempted murder of insufficient consideration for Charley's social advancement.
It would be funny if it weren't so precisely observed.
The Charley passage makes me furious every time — and I think it's meant to.
Charley is the novel's portrait of what respectability costs — he has climbed so hard and so deliberately that he has shed everyone and everything that might slow him down.
Including his sister.
And what's devastating is that he can frame even this — even Bradley's near-murder of Eugene — as a wrong done to himself.
That's what greed of a particular social kind does — it colonises your moral imagination until there's only one person left in the picture.
Greed of the social kind — that's a perfect phrase to carry forward, Caroline.

And I think what today's passages show us — cumulatively — is that Dickens constructs an entire moral spectrum: from the breezy, comic damage of M. R. F.'s predestination schemes, through Bella's genuine transformation, through Wegg's farcical but sinister extortion, through Jenny's transcendent pain, and finally to the psychological depths of Bradley Headstone.
Each registers money, or the absence of it, or the desire for it, differently.
Eleanor, Oliver, Caroline — thank you.
We'll be back shortly with our next segment.
Welcome to this segment of Our Mutual Friend Unpacked, where we turn to the novel's great reckoning of character — what people carry, what they reveal, and what the prose does to make us feel it.
We have three brilliant companions for this conversation.
Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and creative writing teacher who reads Dickens the way a watchmaker reads a movement — always looking for the mechanism beneath the surface.
Oliver Trevelyan has narrated more classic fiction than perhaps any living person — he hears this novel as a performer and brings its voices alive.
And Caroline Woodcourt is a critic and devoted re-reader who has lived with this book since her teens and is never less than fiercely personal about it.
Today we're asking: how does Dickens build character across time — through memory, image, and the telling detail?
Eleanor, you've been looking at passages centred on Boffin — the Golden Dustman — and I want to start with that extraordinary scene where he remembers young John Harmon by the fire.
What strikes me first about this passage is the way Dickens gives Boffin a speaking style that is itself a character portrait.
The parenthetical — 'warming, as fat usually does, with a tendency to melt' — is almost throwaway, and yet it does two things at once.
It gives us the man physically, and it tells us that his emotion is genuine — that he thaws as he remembers.
But then the prose shifts register completely.
Dickens moves into this extraordinary accumulation of short clauses — each one a small blow.
Listen to the build:
'There was his little scanty travelling clothes upon him. There was his little scanty box outside in the shivering wind, which I was going to carry for him down to the steamboat.'
That repetition — 'little scanty,' twice — is doing enormous emotional work with almost no vocabulary.
And then the warmth of Mrs Boffin at the fire, rubbing his cheeks, and then the moment breaks open.
Dickens gives her the most devastating line:
'I'd give the wide wide world, I would, to run away with him!'
That doubling of 'wide' is pure vernacular poetry — it's the kind of intensifier that belongs to feeling, not grammar.
You're absolutely right that this is written for the voice — every word of it.
Boffin speaks in a kind of oral tradition — he is narrating by memory, and the present tense keeps creeping in.
'Mrs Boffin stands him by her, kneels down at the fire, warms her two open hands' — it's all present tense, because for Boffin it still is present.
The memory has never been put down.
And then the novel does something that I find almost unbearable as a performer — it goes even further.
The boy looks up at them both.
'...as if it was in pain—in agony. Such a look!'
Three words — 'Such a look!' — and the narrator practically collapses.
You read that aloud and the room goes quiet.
What moves me most — and I've read this passage many times — is where it ends up.
Because Boffin says that after all of it — after Mrs Boffin waking in the night, calling out — it 'gently wore out, as many things do.'
That qualifier — 'as many things do' — is heartbreaking precisely because it is so calm.
Dickens doesn't editorialize. He just notes it, the way grief actually behaves.
And yet Boffin is telling this story now, which means it hasn't worn out at all — not really.
The Boffins are the moral centre of a novel that is supposedly about money and inheritance.
And the proof of it is in passages like this — and in a much simpler, almost comical moment that I think is one of Dickens's most tender in all the book.
You mean the moment in chapter nine — where Boffin simply tells his wife that it's pleasant to know her.
Dickens sets it up with this magnificent satirical pressure — Mrs Boffin is attempting fashionability, she has social aspirations —
and then her husband says, with complete uncalculated sincerity:
'Yes; and it's pleasant to know that you are Mrs Boffin, and it's been a pleasant thing to know this many and many a year!'
And Dickens then observes — with perfect comic gravity — that this was 'ruin to Mrs Boffin's aspirations.'
They sat together, he writes, 'a hopelessly Unfashionable pair.'
That capital U on 'Unfashionable' — Dickens capitalises the word as if it were an honour.
Which, in his moral universe, it entirely is.
'Hopelessly Unfashionable' — it's one of those Dickensian verdicts that doubles as a benediction.
Now, I want to bring in Sloppy, because I think the novel earns its comedy in precisely the same spirit.
The description of his new suit is an absolute comic set piece — and yet it belongs to the same warmth.
The tailor has been instructed — with great professional seriousness — to conceal the buttons.
But, as Dickens puts it:
'he now stood before the Council, a perfect Argus in the way of buttons: shining and winking and gleaming and twinkling out of a hundred of those eyes of bright metal, at the dazzled spectators.'
The mythology! Argus — the hundred-eyed giant — deployed in the service of a boy who cannot keep his buttons hidden.
It's the grandeur of the reference against the bathos of the subject — that is Dickens at play.
And then the hatband — which 'terminated in a black bunch, from which the imagination shrunk discomfited and the reason revolted.'
I love that. The hat is so bad it defeats both faculties of mind simultaneously.
But Oliver is right — the comedy never mocks Sloppy. It mocks the suit.
Sloppy's form is simply too powerful for tailoring science — there's a kind of bodily heroism in that.
And Mrs Boffin is the one who clothed him. The suit is an act of love that the world resists.
That idea — love that the world resists — runs through the novel's happier passages as well.
There's a scene near the end involving Bella and John Rokesmith and her father, sharing a meal, and it's extraordinary for how deliberately minor it is.
Dickens reaches for a nursery-tale comparison to describe it:
'It was, as Bella gaily said, like the supper provided for the three nursery hobgoblins at their house in the forest, without their thunderous low growlings of the alarming discovery,
He's invoking the fairy-tale frame only to cancel its threat — there will be no growling here, no violation, no dark discovery.
And the iron safe of Chicksey, Veneering, and Stobbles — staring from the corner like 'the eyes of some dull dragon' — is the world's ugliness rendered harmless.
The more uncongenial the surroundings, Dickens says, the more delightful the meal.
That is almost a thesis statement for the whole novel's moral architecture.
Against all of that warmth, the Bradley Headstone passage is like a door slamming shut.
It's the same novelist — but this is Gothic Dickens, and the prose becomes almost sculptural in its coldness.
Bradley sits all night without moving, without speaking — and Dickens watches him deteriorate.
The writing here is almost clinical:

'Rigid before the fire, as if it were a charmed flame that was turning him old, he sat, with the dark lines deepening in his face, its stare becoming more and more haggard, its surface turning whiter and whiter as if it were being overspread with ashes.'
'And the very texture and colour of his hair degenerating.'
That last clause — 'degenerating' — dropped in almost as an afterthought, is devastating.
He's ageing in a single night. The man is being consumed from the inside.
The 'charmed flame' image is the one that stays with me.
Because a charmed flame is not a natural flame — it has intention, it has agency.
The fire is doing this to him. Or something is using the fire to do it.
Compare that to Mrs Boffin kneeling at the fire to warm a child's cheeks — the same element, utterly transformed in moral meaning.
Dickens uses fire to give and fire to consume. The novel knows what it's doing.
That's a precise observation — the novel's imagery is genuinely systematic in that way.
Warmth is the index of goodness here. Its withdrawal — or its perversion into something that destroys — marks damnation.
Bradley is trapped by a fire that ages him rather than shelters him — and notice that he cannot move away from it.
He is 'rigid.' The man who cannot relent, cannot yield, cannot feel warmth as warmth — he simply sits and whitens.
Fire that shelters and fire that consumes — it's a quietly magnificent observation about what this novel does across its entire length.
The Boffins warm a child, the fire turns Bradley to ash — and the novel holds those two images in tension.
Eleanor, Oliver, Caroline — thank you.
In our next segment, we'll be looking at how the novel handles its great social comedy — the Veneerings and their dinner table — and what Dickens means by making society itself the villain.

segments.title: John Harmon's Shadow: Plot, Deception, and Identity

utterances.text: Welcome to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked — the show devoted to one of the most ambitious, strange, and rewarding novels in the English language.

Today's segment goes to the very heart of what makes this novel so unusual: a plot built around a dead man who isn't dead, an identity worn like a disguise, and a narrator who is entirely in on the secret.
We're calling it: John Harmon's Shadow — Plot, Deception, and Identity.
With me to unpack it are three people who know this novel with extraordinary intimacy.
Dr. Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and creative writing teacher who reads every page asking how the thing is built — and why those choices matter.
Oliver Trevelyan has narrated more classic novels in audio than almost anyone alive, and he comes to Dickens as a performer — hearing the rhythms, catching the timing, alive to every voice.

And Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who first read this novel as a teenager and has never quite left it — she reads with her whole heart, and she will tell you exactly which characters deserve better.
Let's begin with the Boffins — because to understand John Harmon's shadow, you first have to understand who loved him before the novel even begins.
What I find endlessly striking about this novel is that John Harmon — the supposed hero — is dead before page one.
Or rather, everyone believes he is dead.
And the foundation of that dramatic irony is laid in the earliest chapters — through the Boffins, who knew the real boy.
Boffin's account of standing up to old Harmon is one of the funniest and most touching passages in the book — simultaneously absurd and completely heartbreaking.
He gives us this extraordinary detail — Dickens simply cannot resist it —
"she wore, in general, a black straw, perched as a matter of convenience on the top of her head."
That parenthesis is doing so much work — pure comic relief inside a scene of genuine cruelty.
And then — "Which dropped her, Mr Lightwood. Dropped her." — two words repeated, and the comedy dissolves completely into something awful.
That repetition — "Dropped her" — is one of those moments where Dickens's voice suddenly strips itself bare.
All the comic energy of the bonnet, the yard, the spinning — and then that monosyllabic thud.
It's the rhythm of shock. Of someone who still can't quite believe it happened.
And what moves me most is what it tells us about young John Harmon — that these two people fought for him, at real cost to themselves, against a monstrous father.
When Rokesmith — who is John, secretly — moves into the Boffins' household, there's a layer of grief in it that the Boffins don't even know is there.
He's watching the people who loved him mourn him. That's devastating.
And Dickens doubles down on that tenderness in the very next chapter — with a passage of authorial reflection that is almost theological in its scope.
He steps back from the Boffins and says something extraordinary about what they represent.
He describes them as "ignorant and unpolished" — and that phrasing is doing double work, because Dickens is actually making a pointed case for moral intelligence over social refinement.
And then he arrives at what I think is one of the great epigrammatic lines in all of Victorian fiction.
"For, Evil often stops short at itself and dies with the doer of it; but Good, never."
That comma before 'never' — the way it isolates the word — is a masterclass in how punctuation creates rhythm and weight.
The sentence earns its grandiosity because the Boffins have earned it — on the page, in action, just paragraphs before.
As someone who has read that line aloud in a studio — the temptation to over-emphasise it is enormous, and entirely wrong.
The line trusts its own structure. You give it space and step back.
What I love is that Dickens plants this moral statement right at the moment when the Boffins are about to do something deeply generous — Mrs Boffin's idea to adopt an orphan and name him John Harmon.
She says it so simply. So quietly. It's the proof of the epigram.
"Now that he is past all benefit of the money, and it's come to us, I should like to find some orphan child, and take the boy and adopt him and give him John's name, and provide for him."
The grammar itself is generous — all those 'and's, accumulating, refusing to stop.
As if the giving can't quite end.
And what makes that moment almost unbearable — in the best possible sense — is what the reader suspects but Mrs Boffin doesn't yet know.
John Harmon is alive. He will enter this household. He will hear her speak his name.
Dickens is constructing a dramatic irony so layered it's almost architectural.
And it connects to what Eleanor said about the epigram — good doesn't die with the doer. It persists. It pulls the living toward the dead.
Which brings us to what Dickens himself says about the whole construction — the authorial note he embeds in the postscript, addressing the reader directly about John Harmon's identity.
It's a remarkable piece of meta-narrative — Dickens defending his craft against readers who thought they'd caught him out.
He writes, with characteristic confidence —

"I foresaw the likelihood that a class of readers and commentators would suppose that I was at great pains to conceal exactly what I was at great pains to suggest: namely, that Mr John Harmon was not slain, and that Mr John Rokesmith was he."
The chiastic elegance of that — 'conceal exactly what I was at great pains to suggest' — is itself a structural demonstration of his argument.
He's saying: the ambiguity was the point. The open secret was intentional. Trust the artist.
'Trust the artist' — from the man who was serialising monthly and absolutely under pressure. It's cheeky and magnificent simultaneously.
But he's right, isn't he? Because when you trace it through — the longing that Rokesmith carries for Bella Wilfer — it's all right there on the page, if you choose to see it.
There's a passage where the narrator gives us Rokesmith's private thought — and it's so piercing in its mixture of tenderness and self-denial.
"If I were but legally executor of Johnny's will! If I had but the right to pay your legacy and to take your receipt!"
He's longing to be himself. To claim his own name. And he frames it in the cold language of inheritance law.
That is a man who has been taught by his entire life to understand love as a legal transaction — and is slowly, painfully, unlearning it.
The 'boofer lady' framing that surrounds it adds such strange tenderness — it's the language of a child, the private nickname, surfacing inside this very adult anguish.
And then the train — all those stations shutting their green eyes and opening their red ones.
The whole world is watching Bella Wilfer pass, and John Harmon — the man who loves her — can only watch from behind his own disguise.
It's one of the most romantically painful images in Dickens. And it passes in barely two sentences.
That compression is the key to the whole novel's technique, I think.
Dickens hides his most emotionally loaded moments inside apparently incidental passages — a train journey, a parenthesis about a bonnet.

And it connects to his method with Riderhood — a character at the other extreme of the novel's moral universe — where the narrator describes Riderhood's predatory skill with almost admiring precision.
"He was a better follower than Bradley. It had been the calling of his life to slink and skulk and dog and waylay, and he knew his calling well."
Four verbs — slink, skulk, dog, waylay — each one a life lived in the shadows of other people's existence.
John Harmon is also a follower of a kind — living in the shadow of his own name, watching from concealment.
The moral distance between Rokesmith and Riderhood is enormous — and yet structurally, in this novel, they're doing something formally similar.
That's a genuinely disturbing comparison — and I mean that as the highest possible compliment to Dickens.
The novel keeps placing its characters in these uncomfortable structural rhymes — who follows, who hides, who watches.
And all of it turns on the question of identity — what name you carry, whether that name is a gift or a cage.
The name as gift or cage — that's the shadow the whole novel lives under, and we've barely scratched the surface of how Dickens manages that.
We'll continue tracing these threads — identity, deception, and what it costs to wear someone else's name — as the episode unfolds.
My thanks to Eleanor Hartley, Oliver Trevelyan, and Caroline Woodcourt — and to you, for listening.

segments.title: Laughter in the Shadows: Dickens's Comic Architecture

utterances.text: Welcome to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked, the show that takes Dickens's last completed novel apart — carefully, lovingly — to see how it works.
I'm your host, and today we're looking at something that makes Our Mutual Friend unlike almost any other Victorian novel: the way its comedy and its darkness are genuinely inseparable.
Joining me today are three brilliant readers of this book, each of whom brings a completely different set of eyes — and ears — to the text.
Dr. Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and creative writing teacher who cares obsessively about how effects are constructed — the architecture behind the magic.
Oliver Trevelyan has read more classic novels aloud for audio than perhaps anyone alive, and he hears the prose the way a musician hears a score.
And Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who first read Our Mutual Friend as a teenager and has been returning to it ever since — with strong opinions about which characters deserve better.
Oliver, let's start with you, because comedy in this novel is really your territory today.
The thing I always say when I'm preparing to read Dickens aloud is: trust the timing.
He has already done the work for you.
And nowhere is that clearer than in the scene where the orphan — little Sloppy — comes tumbling out of Mrs Higden's doorway.
Dickens sets it up so beautifully — the quickened pace, the overbalancing, the topple into the street.
And then he delivers this line, which I defy anyone to read with a straight face.
"Being an orphan of a chubby conformation, he then took to rolling, and had rolled into the gutter before they could come up."
That word — conformation.
It's a word for livestock, or for the shape of a horse.
And applying it to a rolling orphan is — well, it's perfect.
What strikes me there is how much comic work the passive voice is doing.
The orphan doesn't roll — he "took to rolling."
As if rolling were a perfectly natural vocation he had just discovered in himself.
And then Dickens turns the screw further — the meeting with Mrs Higden is "inaugurated" by their being in possession of the orphan, upside down and purple in the countenance.
Inaugurated — a word of grand ceremony applied to a scene of domestic chaos.
That incongruity of register is Dickens's comic engine running at full capacity.
And it doesn't stop there.
There's the board across the doorway, acting as a trap for everyone going in and out simultaneously.
The whole situation is engineered to be maximally undignified for everyone involved.
But what moves me is the phrase at the end: "the cries of the orphan imparted a lugubrious and inhuman character."
Lugubrious and inhuman.
This is a scared toddler screaming in the gutter, and the comedy never entirely smothers that.
The tenderness and the absurdity exist in the same breath, which is very much what this novel does.
And then — and this is what I adore about Sloppy as a character — just a few pages later, Betty Higden sings his praises.
He reads the newspaper to her, she tells us.
And then she says, in five words that became one of the most famous lines in the novel —
"He do the Police in different voices."
Five words.
And they do everything at once: they give us Betty's voice, Sloppy's gift, the poverty that makes a newspaper into an entertainment, and a kind of joy.
T.S. Eliot borrowed that line for a poem title, which is the highest possible tribute.
That line is interesting precisely because the grammar is wrong in exactly the right way.
"He do" — not "he does."
Dickens is rendering Betty Higden's dialect and her class position in the verb form itself.
And simultaneously he's giving her — and Sloppy — enormous dignity.
She's proud of him.
Unambiguously, deeply proud of this boy who does the Police in different voices.
It's also funny in the most particular way — the Police reports, of all things.
Not poetry, not novels — the crime news.
And Sloppy performs them — different voices.
There's something so warm and specific about that detail that it makes me want to cry, frankly.
These characters are poor and precarious, and they have made this beautiful small thing for themselves.
And that balance — between the comic grotesque and the genuinely tender — is something Dickens sustains across very different kinds of scenes in this novel.
Oliver, there's another scene I'd love you to take us to — Wegg and Venus, and what I can only describe as a financial rapture.
Silas Wegg is one of the great comic villains in all of fiction, and that's a strong claim but I stand by it entirely.
He has that wooden leg, the pretensions to literacy, the extraordinary gift for self-importance.
And here, as he and Venus are reading — or mis-reading — a document they think will make them rich, Dickens gives us this physical comedy of the highest order.
The wooden leg elevating itself — gradually, involuntarily — as his excitement mounts.
And the elbow nudging poor Venus deeper and deeper.
Until, inevitably, physics wins.
He drops sideways onto Venus, squeezes him against the settle's edge — and neither of them moves.
"Both remaining in a kind of pecuniary swoon."
Pecuniary swoon.
Two greedy men, collapsed together like toppled statues, overcome by the mere prospect of money.
It's a perfect example of Dickens externalising an internal state through the body.
He doesn't say Wegg is excited by greed.
He shows the wooden leg going up — as if greed were a hydraulic force operating on the man from below.
The comedy is also moral anatomy.
Wegg is dehumanised by his own avarice — his body obeys the money, not the man.
And when the reckoning finally comes for Wegg — when Harmon has had enough of him — it's physical again, isn't it.
There's a wonderful scene where Wegg is mid-sneer, full of himself as always, and then —
"he found himself gripped by the cravat; shaken until his teeth chattered; shoved back, staggering, into a corner of the room; and pinned there."
The syntax mimics the action — four swift blows, each verb landing harder than the last.
It's enormously satisfying.
The reader has been waiting for that for about four hundred pages.
Dickens has been storing up that moment.
Wegg's boundless amazement is the whole point — the man who calculated every angle has been blindsided entirely.
And after that long swoon in pecuniary rapture, to be gripped by the cravat — it's almost balletic in its justice.
There's a line to put next to the "pecuniary swoon" — the arc from delusion to reckoning told entirely through what happens to his body.
That arc is what separates Dickens's comedy from mere farce.
Farce is self-contained — the pratfall happens and is forgotten.
But Dickens's comic scenes are structurally load-bearing.
The rolling orphan tells us something true about the precariousness of childhood in poverty.
The pecuniary swoon tells us something true about what greed does to people.
The comedy is the argument.
Before we close this section, Oliver, I have to bring in one more scene — because it might be the novel's most extraordinary mixture of comedy and genuine feeling.
Mrs Boffin's account of why John Harmon kept delaying the revelation.
This passage — I've read it for audio twice and both times I had to stop.
Not because it's difficult.
Because it catches you completely off guard.
Mrs Boffin is explaining why John kept putting off the great revelation — and his reasoning keeps repeating with this wonderful insistent refrain.
"She is such a cheerful, glorious housewife that I can't afford to be rich yet.
I must wait a little longer."
And it happens again — and again — each time with a new reason.
Until Mrs Boffin has to threaten to turn Informer just to get the man to act.
It is the funniest love letter I have ever encountered inside a novel.
"I can't afford to be rich yet."
That inversion of wealth as something withheld for love — it undoes the whole logic of the novel's world.
The entire plot is driven by inheritance, by the corrupting pull of money.
And here is a man who keeps choosing not to be rich — because she's too good to be rewarded with mere wealth.
Mrs Boffin delivers it as comedy, and it is comedy — but it's heartbreaking too.
What Dickens does with that refrain is structurally audacious.
Repetition in comedy is timing.
But repetition in sentiment is accumulation.
Each repetition of "I must wait a little longer" adds weight — it stops being a joke and becomes a portrait of a man in love.
By the third or fourth time, you realise you've been moved without quite noticing it happen.
That phrase — moved without noticing — feels like a very precise description of what Dickens does throughout Our Mutual Friend.
He gets under your defences while you're laughing.
In our next segment, we're going to look at the novel's darker architecture — the Thames, the dust-heaps, and what this book says about wealth and death.

segments.title: The Heart Beneath the Surface: Character and Conscience

utterances.text: Welcome to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked, the podcast that takes Dickens's last completed novel seriously — as seriously as it deserves.
I'm your host, and today we're deep inside the novel's moral engine — the question of who people really are beneath the roles they perform.
Joining me are three extraordinary readers of this novel.
Dr Eleanor Hartley is a literary critic and novelist who reads Dickens the way a watchmaker reads a movement — for the precision of every working part.
Oliver Trevelyan has narrated more classic novels on audio than almost anyone alive, and he hears this prose the way it was always meant — as performance.

And Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic and devoted re-reader of Our Mutual Friend who brings what no amount of scholarship can manufacture — a reader's instinct for where the novel breaks your heart.
Today we're in the chapters where John Harmon — the man the novel has kept hidden in plain sight — finally accounts for himself.
And Boffin, that magnificent man, delivers a tirade about charitable pretension that is one of the great comic speeches in all of Dickens.
Eleanor, let's begin with John Harmon's confession — this extraordinary chapter where he talks to himself, reasons with himself, persuades himself.
What strikes me first is the almost juridical structure of that confession.
John Harmon isn't just remembering — he's cross-examining himself.
The passage keeps doubling back on itself with that instruction: 'stop, and so far think it out, John Harmon.'
And then comes his own verdict — 'Is that so? That is exactly so.'
It's Dickens building a self-interrogation into the very syntax.
But the emotional weight hangs in that list of what he came back shrinking from.
'I came back, shrinking from my father's money, shrinking from my father's memory, mistrustful of being forced on a mercenary wife.'
That triple repetition of 'shrinking' — it's almost a physical recoil built into the prose rhythm.
The performer in me hears something even more specific in that list.
Each iteration of 'mistrustful' lands on a different target — the wife, the father's intention, himself.
By the time you reach 'mistrustful that I was already growing avaricious' — the suspicion has turned inward entirely.
He has come to distrust his own soul under his father's influence.
And what's brilliant for a narrator is that Dickens doesn't let you outside him for a single clause.
You are trapped inside that consciousness — circling, doubting, reasoning.
What moves me is the mention of his sister.
She appears so briefly — 'my heartbroken sister' — but she haunts everything.
His gratitude to the Boffins is bound up entirely in her memory.
They were, he says, 'the only sunlight in my childish life or that of my heartbroken sister.'
That phrase — the only sunlight — lands with such quiet devastation.
It reframes the whole Boffin plot: his loyalty to them isn't sentimentality — it's a debt of the deepest kind.
And that debt is precisely what makes his deception so structurally complex.
Because by the time he considers coming back to life, he can't do it without harming either Bella or the Boffins.
Dickens frames it as a genuine trap — not a contrived one.
The key passage is this one — listen to how it's constructed.

'When in the distrust engendered by his wretched childhood and the action for evil — never yet for good within his knowledge then — of his father and his father's wealth on all within their influence, he conceived the idea of his first deception, it was meant to be harmless, it was to last but a few hours or days.'
The parenthetical — 'never yet for good within his knowledge then' — is the whole novel's verdict on his father in eight words.
That parenthetical is almost brutal in its compression.
Dickens writes the whole indictment of the father in an aside, mid-sentence — as if it's barely worth slowing down for.
And then the plot logic unfolds — step by step — each step making the next one almost inevitable.
'He confusedly accepted the aid that fell upon him, without considering how firmly it must seem to fix the Boffins in their accession to the fortune.'
'Confusedly' is the key word there — it exonerates him morally even while confirming his complicity.
Dickens is doing something quite subtle — showing us a man who drifted into a deception the way most of us drift into our worst decisions.
That idea of drifting is so important, isn't it.
Dickens says it plainly at the start of that chapter — he had lapsed into his condition 'without perceiving the accumulative power of its separate circumstances.'
That phrase — accumulative power — feels true to life in a way that a neat moral scheme never does.
And then there's the question he asks himself about Bella.
He heard from her own lips that the marriage would have been mercenary.
He then tried her as Rokesmith, and she rejected him.
So he's left asking: 'Was it for him to have the shame of buying her, or the meanness of punishing her?'
Two exits from the trap — both dishonorable.
The trap is perfectly constructed — and what springs him from it is Bella herself changing.
Which brings us to the passage where Harmon, still lying injured in that public house, conceives his plan.
Eleanor, what does Dickens reveal about the nature of that plan — and the moral weight it carries?
The plan arrives in this remarkable formulation — and I want to read it carefully.
'The thought entered my head of turning the danger I had passed through, to the account of being for some time supposed to have disappeared mysteriously, and of proving Bella.'
'Proving Bella' — two words that carry the whole scheme.
And notice: 'the danger I had passed through' isn't described — it's converted immediately into an instrument.
He transforms near-death into an experiment — which is either deeply pragmatic or faintly chilling, depending on how you read it.
But what motivates it isn't cynicism — it's what he calls 'moral timidity that dates from my childhood.'
'Moral timidity' — it's such a devastating self-diagnosis.
And what it's really about is the fear of replicating the curse.
He speaks of 'perpetuating the fate that seemed to have fallen on my father's riches — the fate that they should lead to nothing but evil.'
That's the fear driving the whole deception — not malice, not selfishness, but a dread of money's contaminating power.
Which makes him the opposite of the usual Dickens villain with money.
And yet — I'll admit this — it still troubles me slightly.
He is testing a woman without her knowledge or consent.
However understandable the motive — however rooted in childhood trauma — there's something in that 'proving Bella' that gives me pause.
She is being assessed rather than known.
The novel does vindicate him — Bella genuinely transforms.
But Dickens asks you to feel the discomfort as well as the relief.
That tension is deliberate, I think — and it's what gives the plot its ethical seriousness.
If we were entirely comfortable with John Harmon's choices, there'd be no moral drama.
Dickens makes us see that his intentions towards Bella were, in his own word, 'honestly meant well towards her.'
But intentions and effects are not the same thing — and this novel knows that better than almost any other.
Before we leave these chapters, we must — absolutely must — give Boffin his moment.
Because right beside all this interiority and moral reckoning, Dickens plants one of the great comic outbursts of the whole novel.
Oliver — this one is yours by right.
Mr Boffin on charitable patronage — I have been waiting for this moment.
Because this speech is a piece of comic writing that absolutely requires the human voice to reach its full absurdity.
The setup: Rokesmith is drowning in charitable solicitations, and Boffin has opinions.

'Patrons and Patronesses, and Vice-Patrons and Vice-Patronesses, and Deceased Patrons and Deceased Patronesses, and Ex-Vice-Patrons and Ex-Vice-Patronesses, what does it all mean in the books of the Charities that come pouring in on Rokesmith as he sits among 'em pretty well up to his neck!'
The categories just keep multiplying — Deceased, Ex-Vice — and the whole edifice collapses under its own pomposity.
And then Boffin delivers the killing stroke: 'If it ain't stark staring impudence, what do you call it?'
The Golden Dustman at full throttle — priceless.
What I love is that Boffin is entirely, gloriously right.
The five-shilling donor demanding to be a Patron — Dickens saw it in 1865 and it has not aged a day.
'If Mr Tom Noakes gives his five shillings ain't he a Patron, and if Mrs Jack Styles gives her five shillings ain't she a Patroness?'
The names are perfect — Tom Noakes and Jack Styles — utterly ordinary people dressed in borrowed grandeur.
And the comedy is entirely in Boffin's bewilderment — his genuineness exposing the pretension.
And notice that this speech appears right beside the Harmon chapters — it's not accidental placement.
You have Harmon wrestling agonizingly with wealth's capacity for harm — and then Boffin exploding at the same theme from a completely different angle.
Money corrupts — through inherited curses, through the vanity of charitable display, through every possible avenue.
Dickens is holding both registers simultaneously — the tragic and the farcical — and making them comment on each other.
That double register — the tragic and the comic held in the same breath — is Dickens at his most characteristic.
A man recovering from near-death, devising an experiment in human character — and on the next page, the Golden Dustman roaring at fake Patronesses.
Our Mutual Friend contains multitudes, and that is precisely why we keep returning to it.
My thanks to Eleanor Hartley, Oliver Trevelyan, and Caroline Woodcourt — we'll be back shortly with the next segment.

segments.title: Closing: What Our Mutual Friend Reveals

utterances.text: We've spent this episode moving through some of the most charged passages in Our Mutual Friend — the river, the money, the disguises, the slow work of becoming a better self.
As we close, I want to ask each of you what this novel ultimately reveals — about us, about the society Dickens is dissecting, about what fiction can do.
Eleanor, let's begin with you — and with that extraordinary opening image of Gaffer and the river.
What Dickens reveals, I think, is the ceremony of greed.
Gaffer pulls money from a dead man, and what does he do?
He performs a ritual over it — washing it, cherishing it, blessing it.
Dickens gives us the sentence that captures the whole novel's obsession — listen to it:
"He chinked it once, and he blew upon it once, and he spat upon it once,—'for luck,' he hoarsely said—before he put it in his pocket."
Three verbs in perfect sequence — chinked, blew, spat — like a dark liturgy.
The novel opens with money drawn from a corpse, and that is not metaphor — it is the engine of every plot that follows.
Eleanor is absolutely right about that liturgy — and as a performer, I feel it in the mouth.
Those three short beats — chink, blow, spit — they're comic and hideous at the same time.
That 'hoarsely said' is doing tremendous work — Gaffer's voice is the voice of the river itself, rasping and amoral.
And what the novel reveals — on every page, in every drawing room and dustheap — is that nobody is innocent of money.
The Veneerings buying their friends, Bella Wilfer aspiring upward, Gaffer fishing corpses for coin — it's the same story at every level of society.
What stays with me — what always stays with me — is the children.
There is a passage where Lizzie describes a small, ailing girl, and what surrounds her from birth.
"This poor ailing little creature has come to be what she is, surrounded by drunken people from her cradle—if she ever had one, Charley."
That parenthesis — 'if she ever had one' — breaks my heart every time.
Dickens slides it in almost casually, and then you feel the full weight of it.
A cradle — such an ordinary thing — and the possibility that this child never had one.
That is what Our Mutual Friend reveals — the human cost that polite society never looks at directly.
And Dickens keeps insisting — structurally, relentlessly — that these worlds are not separate.
Take the Harmon plot — John Harmon dressing as a common sailor, moving through Bella Wilfer's neighbourhood to test whether she's genuine.
Here is how Harmon describes the scheme:

"the plot was made out of our getting common sailors' dresses (as he was able to guide me about London), and throwing ourselves in Bella Wilfer's neighbourhood, and trying to put ourselves in her way."
Identity in this novel is a costume — put on, taken off, tested against reality.
Class, character, love — all of it subject to disguise and revelation.
And the wonderful, painful irony is that even Harmon's sincerity — his genuine desire to know Bella truly — begins with a deception.
You cannot arrive at authenticity in this novel without first passing through performance.
And I think that is what Dickens understands about human beings — that we are always, to some degree, in costume.
The question is whether the person underneath is worth finding.
And Lizzie Hexam's answer — without ever stating it as a thesis — is yes.
Surrounded by every degradation the novel can imagine, she remains — fiercely, quietly — herself.
That is the moral anchor of the whole book, for me.
Ceremony, cost, costume — and underneath it all, the question of character.
Our Mutual Friend asks whether what we are made of can survive what the world makes of us.
It's a question Dickens poses in the novel's very first paragraph, with money drawn from a corpse in a dark river — and answers, slowly, over nine hundred pages.
My deepest thanks to Eleanor Hartley, Oliver Trevelyan, and Caroline Woodcourt for a conversation as rich as the novel itself.
For Our Mutual Friend Unpacked, I'm your host — and we'll see you next time.

c17:p4.text:
But no one knows so well as the Secretary, who opens and reads the
      letters, what a set is made at the man marked by a stroke of notoriety. Oh
      the varieties of dust for ocular use, offered in exchange for the gold
      dust of the Golden Dustman! Fifty-seven churches to be erected with
      half-crowns, forty-two parsonage houses to be repaired with shillings,
      seven-and-twenty organs to be built with halfpence, twelve hundred
      children to be brought up on postage stamps. Not that a half-crown,
      shilling, halfpenny, or postage stamp, would be particularly acceptable
      from Mr Boffin, but that it is so obvious he is the man to make up the
      deficiency. And then the charities, my Christian brother! And mostly in
      difficulties, yet mostly lavish, too, in the expensive articles of print
      and paper. Large fat private double letter, sealed with ducal coronet.
      ‘Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire. My Dear Sir,—Having consented to preside
      at the forthcoming Annual Dinner of the Family Party Fund, and feeling
      deeply impressed with the immense usefulness of that noble Institution and
      the great importance of its being supported by a List of Stewards that
      shall prove to the public the interest taken in it by popular and
      distinguished men, I have undertaken to ask you to become a Steward on
      that occasion. Soliciting your favourable reply before the 14th instant, I
      am, My Dear Sir, Your faithful Servant,  Linseed . P.S. The Steward’s fee is
      limited to three Guineas.’ Friendly this, on the part of the Duke of
      Linseed (and thoughtful in the postscript), only lithographed by the
      hundred and presenting but a pale individuality of an address to Nicodemus
      Boffin, Esquire, in quite another hand. It takes two noble Earls and a
      Viscount, combined, to inform Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire, in an equally
      flattering manner, that an estimable lady in the West of England has
      offered to present a purse containing twenty pounds, to the Society for
      Granting Annuities to Unassuming Members of the Middle Classes, if twenty
      individuals will previously present purses of one hundred pounds each. And
      those benevolent noblemen very kindly point out that if Nicodemus Boffin,
      Esquire, should wish to present two or more purses, it will not be
      inconsistent with the design of the estimable lady in the West of England,
      provided each purse be coupled with the name of some member of his
      honoured and respected family.
c17:p4.summary: The Secretary describes the flood of charitable solicitations and scheme proposals that inundate the Boffins, including a satirical example of a duke's letter requesting Boffin become a Steward of a charity for a three-guinea fee.
c17:p4.best_quote: Large fat private double letter, sealed with ducal coronet.

c17:p5.text:
These are the corporate beggars. But there are, besides, the individual
      beggars; and how does the heart of the Secretary fail him when he has to
      cope with  them!  And they must be coped with to some extent, because they
      all enclose documents (they call their scraps documents; but they are, as
      to papers deserving the name, what minced veal is to a calf), the
      non-return of which would be their ruin. That is to say, they are utterly
      ruined now, but they would be more utterly ruined then. Among these
      correspondents are several daughters of general officers, long accustomed
      to every luxury of life (except spelling), who little thought, when their
      gallant fathers waged war in the Peninsula, that they would ever have to
      appeal to those whom Providence, in its inscrutable wisdom, has blessed
      with untold gold, and from among whom they select the name of Nicodemus
      Boffin, Esquire, for a maiden effort in this wise, understanding that he
      has such a heart as never was. The Secretary learns, too, that confidence
      between man and wife would seem to obtain but rarely when virtue is in
      distress, so numerous are the wives who take up their pens to ask Mr
      Boffin for money without the knowledge of their devoted husbands, who
      would never permit it; while, on the other hand, so numerous are the
      husbands who take up their pens to ask Mr Boffin for money without the
      knowledge of their devoted wives, who would instantly go out of their
      senses if they had the least suspicion of the circumstance. There are the
      inspired beggars, too. These were sitting, only yesterday evening, musing
      over a fragment of candle which must soon go out and leave them in the
      dark for the rest of their nights, when surely some Angel whispered the
      name of Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire, to their souls, imparting rays of hope,
      nay confidence, to which they had long been strangers! Akin to these are
      the suggestively-befriended beggars. They were partaking of a cold potato
      and water by the flickering and gloomy light of a lucifer-match, in their
      lodgings (rent considerably in arrear, and heartless landlady threatening
      expulsion ‘like a dog’ into the streets), when a gifted friend happening
      to look in, said, ‘Write immediately to Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire,’ and
      would take no denial. There are the nobly independent beggars too. These,
      in the days of their abundance, ever regarded gold as dross, and have not
      yet got over that only impediment in the way of their amassing wealth, but
      they want no dross from Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire; No, Mr Boffin; the
      world may term it pride, paltry pride if you will, but they wouldn’t take
      it if you offered it; a loan, sir—for fourteen weeks to the day,
      interest calculated at the rate of five per cent per annum, to be bestowed
      upon any charitable institution you may name—is all they want of
      you, and if you have the meanness to refuse it, count on being despised by
      these great spirits. There are the beggars of punctual business-habits
      too. These will make an end of themselves at a quarter to one P.M. on
      Tuesday, if no Post-office order is in the interim received from Nicodemus
      Boffin, Esquire; arriving after a quarter to one P.M. on Tuesday, it need
      not be sent, as they will then (having made an exact memorandum of the
      heartless circumstances) be ‘cold in death.’ There are the beggars on
      horseback too, in another sense from the sense of the proverb. These are
      mounted and ready to start on the highway to affluence. The goal is before
      them, the road is in the best condition, their spurs are on, the steed is
      willing, but, at the last moment, for want of some special thing—a
      clock, a violin, an astronomical telescope, an electrifying machine—they
      must dismount for ever, unless they receive its equivalent in money from
      Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire. Less given to detail are the beggars who make
      sporting ventures. These, usually to be addressed in reply under initials
      at a country post-office, inquire in feminine hands, Dare one who cannot
      disclose herself to Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire, but whose name might
      startle him were it revealed, solicit the immediate advance of two hundred
      pounds from unexpected riches exercising their noblest privilege in the
      trust of a common humanity?
c17:p5.summary: The Secretary catalogs individual beggars seeking Boffin's charity—daughters of officers, distressed wives and husbands, those claiming divine inspiration, independent beggars offering loans, and those threatening suicide—each category satirically anatomized.
c17:p5.best_quote: they call their scraps documents; but they are, as to papers deserving the name, what minced veal is to a calf

‘Exactly so, sir!’ returned Wegg, blandly and buoyantly. ‘I see I take you
      with me! Hear, hear, hear! Resolved, as your discriminating good sense
      perceives, that if you was to have a sap—pur— ize , it should be
      a complete one! Well, sir. And so, as you have honoured me by
      anticipating, I examined the document. Regularly executed, regularly
      witnessed, very short. Inasmuch as he has never made friends, and has ever
      had a rebellious family, he, John Harmon, gives to Nicodemus Boffin the

      Estate. But when my second brother was going to be born by-and-by, “this,”
       says M. R. F., “is a little pillar of the church.”  Was  born, and became a
      pillar of the church; a very shaky one. My third brother appeared,
      considerably in advance of his engagement to my mother; but M. R. F., not
      at all put out by surprise, instantly declared him a Circumnavigator. Was
      pitch-forked into the Navy, but has not circumnavigated. I announced
      myself and was disposed of with the highly satisfactory results embodied
      before you. When my younger brother was half an hour old, it was settled
      by M. R. F. that he should have a mechanical genius. And so on. Therefore
      I say that M. R. F. amuses me.’

‘And therefore—and therefore,’ the cherub went on in a glowing

      mercenary young person distantly related to myself, refused the price,
      took off the splendid fashions that were part of it, put on the

c40:p72.text:
On this head, Silas Wegg had much to say. Silas had to say That, he would
      beg to remind his comrade, brother, and partner, of the impressive
      passages they had read that evening; of the evident parallel in Mr
      Boffin’s mind between them and the late owner of the Bower, and the
      present circumstances of the Bower; of the bottle; and of the box. That,
      the fortunes of his brother and comrade, and of himself were evidently
      made, inasmuch as they had but to put their price upon this document, and
      get that price from the minion of fortune and the worm of the hour: who
      now appeared to be less of a minion and more of a worm than had been
      previously supposed. That, he considered it plain that such price was
      stateable in a single expressive word, and that the word was, ‘Halves!’
      That, the question then arose when ‘Halves!’ should be called. That, here
      he had a plan of action to recommend, with a conditional clause. That, the
      plan of action was that they should lie by with patience; that, they
      should allow the Mounds to be gradually levelled and cleared away, while
      retaining to themselves their present opportunity of watching the process—which
      would be, he conceived, to put the trouble and cost of daily digging and
      delving upon somebody else, while they might nightly turn such complete
      disturbance of the dust to the account of their own private investigations—and
      that, when the Mounds were gone, and they had worked those chances for
      their own joint benefit solely, they should then, and not before, explode
      on the minion and worm. But here came the conditional clause, and to this
      he entreated the special attention of his comrade, brother, and partner.
      It was not to be borne that the minion and worm should carry off any of
      that property which was now to be regarded as their own property. When he,
      Mr Wegg, had seen the minion surreptitiously making off with that bottle,
      and its precious contents unknown, he had looked upon him in the light of
      a mere robber, and, as such, would have despoiled him of his ill-gotten
      gain, but for the judicious interference of his comrade, brother, and
      partner. Therefore, the conditional clause he proposed was, that, if the
      minion should return in his late sneaking manner, and if, being closely
      watched, he should be found to possess himself of anything, no matter
      what, the sharp sword impending over his head should be instantly shown
      him, he should be strictly examined as to what he knew or suspected,
      should be severely handled by them his masters, and should be kept in a
      state of abject moral bondage and slavery until the time when they should
      see fit to permit him to purchase his freedom at the price of half his
      possessions. If, said Mr Wegg by way of peroration, he had erred in saying
      only ‘Halves!’ he trusted to his comrade, brother, and partner not to
      hesitate to set him right, and to reprove his weakness. It might be more
      according to the rights of things, to say Two-thirds; it might be more
      according to the rights of things, to say Three-fourths. On those points
      he was ever open to correction.
c40:p72.summary: Wegg proposes an elaborate scheme: let Boffin excavate the Mounds at his own expense while they observe, then when the work is done, threaten him with the earlier will and extort half his property. If Boffin is caught secretly removing anything, they will interrogate and enslave him morally until he pays for his freedom.

c19:p76.text:
‘I dare say my birds sing better than other birds, and my flowers smell
      better than other flowers. For when I was a little child,’ in a tone as
      though it were ages ago, ‘the children that I used to see early in the
      morning were very different from any others that I ever saw. They were not
      like me; they were not chilled, anxious, ragged, or beaten; they were
      never in pain. They were not like the children of the neighbours; they
      never made me tremble all over, by setting up shrill noises, and they
      never mocked me. Such numbers of them too! All in white dresses, and with
      something shining on the borders, and on their heads, that I have never
      been able to imitate with my work, though I know it so well. They used to
      come down in long bright slanting rows, and say all together, “Who is this
      in pain! Who is this in pain!” When I told them who it was, they answered,
      “Come and play with us!” When I said “I never play! I can’t play!” they
      swept about me and took me up, and made me light. Then it was all
      delicious ease and rest till they laid me down, and said, all together,
      “Have patience, and we will come again.” Whenever they came back, I used
      to know they were coming before I saw the long bright rows, by hearing
      them ask, all together a long way off, “Who is this in pain! Who is this
      in pain!” And I used to cry out, “O my blessed children, it’s poor me.
      Have pity on me. Take me up and make me light!”’
c19:p76.summary: Jenny recounts a memory or vision from her childhood of celestial children in white who appeared to her, asking 'Who is this in pain?' and offering her comfort and rest. They promised to return, and their refrain became her solace.

c57:p53.text:
Now, too, was he cursed with a state of mind more wearing and more
      wearisome than remorse. He had no remorse; but the evildoer who can hold
      that avenger at bay, cannot escape the slower torture of incessantly doing
      the evil deed again and doing it more efficiently. In the defensive
      declarations and pretended confessions of murderers, the pursuing shadow
      of this torture may be traced through every lie they tell. If I had done
      it as alleged, is it conceivable that I would have made this and this
      mistake? If I had done it as alleged, should I have left that unguarded
      place which that false and wicked witness against me so infamously deposed
      to? The state of that wretch who continually finds the weak spots in his
      own crime, and strives to strengthen them when it is unchangeable, is a
      state that aggravates the offence by doing the deed a thousand times
      instead of once; but it is a state, too, that tauntingly visits the
      offence upon a sullen unrepentant nature with its heaviest punishment
      every time.
c57:p53.summary: The narrator explores the psychological torment of murderers without remorse: they are compelled to endlessly re-enact and mentally perfect their crime, creating a torture worse than remorse itself.

c57:p86.text:
‘When I speak of my sister, I devoutly wish that you had never seen her,
      Mr Headstone. However, you did see her, and that’s useless now. I confided
      in you about her. I explained her character to you, and how she interposed
      some ridiculous fanciful notions in the way of our being as respectable as
      I tried for. You fell in love with her, and I favoured you with all my
      might. She could not be induced to favour you, and so we came into
      collision with this Mr Eugene Wrayburn. Now, what have you done? Why, you
      have justified my sister in being firmly set against you from first to
      last, and you have put me in the wrong again! And why have you done it?
      Because, Mr Headstone, you are in all your passions so selfish, and so
      concentrated upon yourself that you have not bestowed one proper thought
      on me.’

c8:p43.text:
‘The last time me and Mrs Boffin saw the poor boy,’ said Mr Boffin,
      warming (as fat usually does) with a tendency to melt, ‘he was a child of
      seven year old. For when he came back to make intercession for his sister,
      me and Mrs Boffin were away overlooking a country contract which was to be
      sifted before carted, and he was come and gone in a single hour. I say he
      was a child of seven year old. He was going away, all alone and forlorn,
      to that foreign school, and he come into our place, situate up the yard of
      the present Bower, to have a warm at our fire. There was his little scanty
      travelling clothes upon him. There was his little scanty box outside in
      the shivering wind, which I was going to carry for him down to the
      steamboat, as the old man wouldn’t hear of allowing a sixpence
      coach-money. Mrs Boffin, then quite a young woman and pictur of a
      full-blown rose, stands him by her, kneels down at the fire, warms her two
      open hands, and falls to rubbing his cheeks; but seeing the tears come
      into the child’s eyes, the tears come fast into her own, and she holds him
      round the neck, like as if she was protecting him, and cries to me, “I’d
      give the wide wide world, I would, to run away with him!” I don’t say but
      what it cut me, and but what it at the same time heightened my feelings of
      admiration for Mrs Boffin. The poor child clings to her for awhile, as she
      clings to him, and then, when the old man calls, he says “I must go! God
      bless you!” and for a moment rests his heart against her bosom, and looks
      up at both of us, as if it was in pain—in agony. Such a look! I went
      aboard with him (I gave him first what little treat I thought he’d like),
      and I left him when he had fallen asleep in his berth, and I came back to
      Mrs Boffin. But tell her what I would of how I had left him, it all went
      for nothing, for, according to her thoughts, he never changed that look
      that he had looked up at us two. But it did one piece of good. Mrs Boffin
      and me had no child of our own, and had sometimes wished that how we had
      one. But not now. “We might both of us die,” says Mrs Boffin, “and other
      eyes might see that lonely look in our child.” So of a night, when it was
      very cold, or when the wind roared, or the rain dripped heavy, she would
      wake sobbing, and call out in a fluster, “Don’t you see the poor child’s
      face? O shelter the poor child!”—till in course of years it gently
      wore out, as many things do.’
c8:p43.summary: Boffin recounts the last time he and Mrs Boffin saw young John Harmon, a seven-year-old being sent to a foreign school, including the poignant moment when Mrs Boffin wept while warming the boy by the fire and embraced him protectively, expressing a desire to save him—a memory that haunted her for years.

c9:p28.text:
‘Yes; and it’s pleasant to know that you are Mrs Boffin,’ said her
      husband, ‘and it’s been a pleasant thing to know this many and many a
      year!’ It was ruin to Mrs Boffin’s aspirations, but, having so spoken,

c27:p51.text:
The consideration of Mrs Boffin had clothed Mr Sloppy in a suit of black,
      on which the tailor had received personal directions from Rokesmith to
      expend the utmost cunning of his art, with a view to the concealment of
      the cohering and sustaining buttons. But, so much more powerful were the
      frailties of Sloppy’s form than the strongest resources of tailoring
      science, that he now stood before the Council, a perfect Argus in the way
      of buttons: shining and winking and gleaming and twinkling out of a
      hundred of those eyes of bright metal, at the dazzled spectators. The
      artistic taste of some unknown hatter had furnished him with a hatband of
      wholesale capacity which was fluted behind, from the crown of his hat to
      the brim, and terminated in a black bunch, from which the imagination
      shrunk discomfited and the reason revolted. Some special powers with which
      his legs were endowed, had already hitched up his glossy trousers at the
      ankles, and bagged them at the knees; while similar gifts in his arms had
      raised his coat-sleeves from his wrists and accumulated them at his
      elbows. Thus set forth, with the additional embellishments of a very
      little tail to his coat, and a yawning gulf at his waistband, Sloppy stood
      confessed.

c27:p51.best_quote: he now stood before the Council, a perfect Argus in the way of buttons: shining and winking and gleaming and twinkling out of a hundred of those eyes of bright metal, at the dazzled spectators.

c49:p79.text:
It was, as Bella gaily said, like the supper provided for the three
      nursery hobgoblins at their house in the forest, without their thunderous

c65:p104.text:
Not one other word did Bradley utter all that night. Not once did he
      change his attitude, or loosen his hold upon his wrist. Rigid before the
      fire, as if it were a charmed flame that was turning him old, he sat, with

      overspread with ashes, and the very texture and colour of his hair
      degenerating.
